title: How the sandbox reads English
summary: Lexers, tokens and recursive descent: how compilers read your code.

cards.title: Two steps, like every compiler
cards.body:
The English → Diagram sandbox understands text like "sorted array of 9, 2 and 7". It does it the same way a C++ compiler reads your code:

- The **lexer** cuts characters into **tokens**: words, numbers, arrows, commas.
- The **parser** reads the tokens left to right and decides what they mean.

It's a deliberately tiny language, so forgiving words like "a", "of" and "and" are simply skipped.

cards.title: The lexer
cards.body: Look at the arrow case: two characters (`->`) become one token. And `-4` after a space is a negative number, while `A-4` is an edge. The lexer decides by looking one character back.

cards.title: The parser
cards.body: **Recursive descent**: one small function per part of the grammar (`kind()`, `numbers()`, `operations()`, `edges()`). Each function consumes the tokens it understands and returns. Real compilers are built the same way, with a much bigger grammar.

cards.question: How many tokens does the lexer produce for `list 1 -> 2`?
cards.explain: list, 1, ->, 2: four tokens. The arrow's two characters form one token, and spaces produce none.

cards.question: What does the parser do with the word "of" in "array of 5 3"?
choices: Skips it as a filler word
cards.explain: skipFiller() steps over words like a, an, the, of, with and and. That's what makes the language forgiving.

cards.title: Why this matters for AI apps
cards.body: An AI model asked to "draw a tree of 8, 3 and 10" could answer in this little language instead of free text. The app can then **parse and check** the answer before drawing it: if it doesn't parse, it isn't shown. Constraining a model's output to a language you can validate is one of the most practical ways to make AI features trustworthy.
